title: Given a set of distinct elements, generate all possible orderings (permutations) using backtracking.
shortTitle: Generate All Permutations of a Set (Backtracking)
topicTitle: Explain Merge Sort. Why is it O

s1_definition.profdef: A permutation is an arrangement of all elements of a set in a specific order, and a set of n distinct elements has n factorial permutations. Backtracking generates them by building an arrangement one position at a time, at each position trying every element not yet used, recursing to fill the next position, then undoing the choice to try the next candidate. The algorithm runs in time proportional to n times n factorial because it produces that many arrangements of length n.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must try every possible order of processing a small batch of urgent transfers to find the sequence that best satisfies liquidity rules. A clerk fills a row of slots, one per transfer. In the first slot she tries each transfer in turn; having placed one, she moves to the second slot and tries each remaining transfer, and so on until all slots are filled, giving one complete ordering. Then she pulls the last placed transfer back out and tries the next candidate, systematically producing every possible order without ever repeating a transfer within one arrangement.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill each position with every unused element, recurse, then undo, producing all n factorial orderings.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A permutation is an arrangement of all elements of a set in a specific order, and a set of n distinct elements has n factorial permutations. Backtracking generates them by building an arrangement one position at a time, at each position trying every element not yet used, recursing to fill the next position, then undoing the choice to try the next candidate. The algorithm runs in time proportional to n times n factorial because it produces that many arrangements of length n.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India must try every possible order of processing a small batch of urgent transfers to find the sequence that best satisfies liquidity rules. A clerk fills a row of slots, one per transfer. In the first slot she tries each transfer in turn; having placed one, she moves to the second slot and tries each remaining transfer, and so on until all slots are filled, giving one complete ordering. Then she pulls the last placed transfer back out and tries the next candidate, systematically producing every possible order without ever repeating a transfer within one arrangement.

**One line to remember:** Fill each position with every unused element, recurse, then undo, producing all n factorial orderings.

sections.s2_technical:
Permutations differ from subsets in two ways: order matters, and every arrangement uses all elements. So the decision at each step is not include-or-exclude but "which of the remaining unused elements goes in this position." That requires tracking which elements are already used in the current arrangement.

The standard formulation carries a running path and a used-marker, typically a boolean array parallel to the input. At each call, if the path length equals n you have a complete arrangement and record a copy of it. Otherwise you loop over all elements, skip any that are already used, and for each unused one you mark it used, add it to the path, recurse, then undo by removing it from the path and clearing its used flag. The core is `used[i] = true; path.add(nums[i]); backtrack(...); path.remove(path.size()-1); used[i] = false;`. The skip of used elements is what prevents repeating an element within a single arrangement.

As with subsets, you must store a copy when recording, because the path is mutated across the whole search. Recording only happens at the leaves, when the path is full, unlike subsets which record at every node, and that reflects the difference that a permutation must use all elements.

A senior-level nuance is handling duplicates and the swap-based variant. If the input has repeated elements, you sort it and skip a candidate when it equals the previous one and the previous one is not used, which avoids generating identical permutations. There is also an in-place swap formulation that permutes the array directly without a used array, swapping each element into the current position and swapping back, which saves the auxiliary structure. Permutations appear in scheduling, routing such as brute-force travelling-salesman on tiny inputs, and exhaustive test-case generation, though because the count is factorial it is only feasible for small n, which is itself a key point to state.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's treasury must occasionally evaluate every possible processing order of a very small batch of urgent transfers to pick the sequence that keeps intraday liquidity within limits. This is exactly generating all permutations of the batch.

Problem 2 — Each transfer must appear exactly once per candidate ordering, and every distinct ordering must be produced, so the generator must track used transfers and never repeat one within an arrangement. The used-marker in backtracking enforces that.

In our mini-project we build a `TransferOrderPlanner` that returns all orderings of a small list of transfer IDs using backtracking. The demo generates all orderings of three transfers and logs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three transfers, TXF-1, TXF-2, TXF-3, generating all orderings.

Step 1: Enter backtrack with an empty path. The path length is zero, not three, so we loop. We place TXF-1, mark it used, recurse.

Step 2: Path is TXF-1, length one. Loop again, skip TXF-1 as used, place TXF-2, mark used, recurse. Path is TXF-1, TXF-2. Loop, place TXF-3, path is full, record TXF-1, TXF-2, TXF-3.

Step 3: Backtrack: remove TXF-3, clear its flag, loop ends at that level, remove TXF-2, clear its flag. Back at path TXF-1. Continue the loop, place TXF-3, recurse, then place TXF-2, record TXF-1, TXF-3, TXF-2. Backtrack out to the empty path, clearing TXF-1.

Step 4: Back at the top, place TXF-2 first. Recurse and generate TXF-2, TXF-1, TXF-3 and TXF-2, TXF-3, TXF-1 by the same include-and-undo process.

Step 5: Finally place TXF-3 first and generate TXF-3, TXF-1, TXF-2 and TXF-3, TXF-2, TXF-1.

Step 6: Every position has tried every unused transfer. The result holds all six orderings, exactly three factorial, each using all three transfers once. Each recorded ordering is an independent copy.

[2026-10-26 23:33:01] INFO      order: [TXF-1, TXF-3, TXF-2]

```
  ═══ LLD — Permutations (Backtracking) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Backtracking with used[] marker — order matters              │
  │  Record only at leaves (full-length path)                     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: TransferOrderPlanner only enumerates orderings            │
  │  O: add sort + skip-duplicate to handle repeated elements     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          TransferOrderPlanner         │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + allOrders(transfers[]): List<List> │  O(n · n!)
  │  - backtrack(transfers, used, path, r)│  skip used; undo
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Post: n! distinct orderings, each uses all elements once

  ── State Diagram: Position fill ─────────────────────────

  [path < n] ──pick unused──→ mark used, recurse ──→ undo
  [path == n] ──→ record copy (leaf)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. allOrders → backtrack(used=all false, [])
  2.   if path full → record copy
  3.   for i: if used[i] skip; else mark, add, recurse, undo
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A permutation is an arrangement of all the elements of a set in a specific order, and a set of n distinct elements has n factorial permutations. I generate them with backtracking, building an arrangement one position at a time. At each position I try every element that is not yet used, recurse to fill the next position, then undo the choice so I can try the next candidate. Each time the arrangement reaches full length I have one complete permutation.

The key difference from generating subsets is that order matters and every arrangement uses all elements, so instead of an include-or-exclude decision I ask "which unused element goes here," which means I carry a used-marker alongside the running path. At each call, if the path is full I record a copy and return; otherwise I loop over all elements, skip any already used, and for each unused one I mark it used, add it, recurse, then remove it and clear the flag. That skip of used elements is what stops an element repeating within a single arrangement, and I record only at the leaves because a permutation must be complete. As always I store a copy when recording, since the path is mutated throughout the search.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in treasury, where we occasionally evaluate every possible processing order of a very small batch of urgent transfers to pick the sequence that keeps intraday liquidity within limits. The used-marker ensured each transfer appeared exactly once per ordering and that every distinct ordering was produced.

The senior-level point I always make is about feasibility and duplicates. Because the number of permutations is factorial, this is only viable for small n, and I say that explicitly so the interviewer knows I understand the cost. For inputs with repeated elements I sort first and skip a candidate equal to its predecessor when the predecessor is unused, which prevents identical permutations, and I mention the in-place swap variant that permutes the array directly without a used array to save the auxiliary space.
